meta.title: Russian and Soviet elections
sources: Wikipedia: Russian presidential election articles 1991–2024 and Soviet Union election articles 1922–1990 (results, infoboxes and leads)
CEC figures as reported there — with the caveats each contest deserves

presEras.label: The Soviet presidency
presEras.blurb: The Soviet Union created an executive presidency only in its final year: Mikhail Gorbachev was elected unopposed by the Congress of People's Deputies in March 1990 — the office's first and last holder. By the next winter the state itself was gone.

presEras.label: The Yeltsin elections
presEras.blurb: Russia's June 1991 election — held while the USSR still existed — made Boris Yeltsin the first popularly elected leader in a thousand years of Russian history. The 1996 re-election was genuinely contested but deeply tilted: state television, oligarch money and a manufactured second-round choice against the Communist Zyuganov.

presEras.label: The managed succession
presEras.blurb: Every election since 2000 has kept one man or his placeholder in the Kremlin. The machinery tightened by stages — television first, then candidate registration, then open repression — until 2024's wartime vote, held with every genuine opponent dead, imprisoned or exiled. These are recorded here as the managed rituals they became, not competitive elections.

legEras.label: The imperial Dumas
legEras.blurb: The 1905 revolution forced a parliament from the Tsar: four State Dumas elected through indirect, class-weighted curiae in which a landowner's vote outweighed dozens of peasants'. The first two Dumas proved defiant and were dissolved within months; Stolypin's June 1907 'coup' rewrote the franchise mid-stream, and the tamer Third and Fourth Dumas sat until the empire fell.

legEras.label: Revolution and the Constituent Assembly
legEras.blurb: The November 1917 Constituent Assembly election was Russia's first universal-suffrage national vote — and its last free one until 1991. The Socialist-Revolutionaries won it decisively; the Bolsheviks, who did not, dissolved the assembly after a single day's sitting. By 1921 elections meant indirect soviet votes under a consolidating one-party state.

legEras.label: The Congress of Soviets
legEras.blurb: The early Soviet state elected its congresses indirectly, through soviets, on an openly class-weighted franchise: workers' votes counted five times a peasant's, and 'former people' — priests, merchants, ex-officials — could not vote at all. No opposition to the Communist Party was permitted at any stage.

legEras.label: The Supreme Soviet rituals
legEras.blurb: The 1936 Stalin constitution introduced direct, universal, secret voting — for exactly one candidate per seat, nominated by the party. For half a century the Soviet Union staged the theatre of elections with announced turnouts above 99%. They are recorded here as rituals of the dictatorship, not elections.

legEras.label: The perestroika breakthrough
legEras.blurb: Gorbachev's Congress of People's Deputies election was the first Soviet vote since 1917 with a choice on the ballot. A third of the seats were reserved for the party and its organisations, but in the contested districts voters humiliated party bosses, elected Yeltsin with 89% in Moscow — and started the avalanche that buried the state.

legEras.label: The contested Duma
legEras.blurb: The new constitution's Duma was elected in real, chaotic contests: Zhirinovsky's shock plurality in 1993 — weeks after tanks shelled the old parliament — the Communist wins of 1995 and 1999, and the fractious multiparty chamber they produced. By 2003, when United Russia first swept the board on tilted airwaves, the window was already closing.

legEras.label: The managed Duma
legEras.blurb: Since 2007 the Duma has been a managed chamber: United Russia's supermajorities are assembled through a licensed 'systemic opposition', ballot fraud where needed — the trigger for the 2011–12 protests — and the exclusion of genuine opponents. The announced results are recorded here with that label.

presidential.summary: The 1990 Soviet Union presidential election was held in the Soviet Union on 14 March 1990 to elect a president for a five-year term. This was the first and only presidential election to be held in the Soviet Union.
presidential.caveat: An indirect, uncontested vote of the Congress of People's Deputies — Gorbachev was the only candidate.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR) on 12 June 1991. This was the first ever Russian presidential election.

Presidential elections were held in Russia on 16 June 1996, with a second round being held on 3 July 1996. It resulted in a victory for the incumbent Russian president Boris Yeltsin, who ran as an independent politician.
presidential.caveat: Genuinely contested, but heavily tilted: near-total state and oligarch media backing for Yeltsin, and enduring allegations of fraud in both rounds.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Russia on 26 March 2000. Incumbent prime minister and acting president Vladimir Putin, who had succeeded Boris Yeltsin after his resignation on 31 December 1999, sought a four-year term in his own right and won in the first round.
presidential.caveat: Held amid the Second Chechen War with state television campaigning for the incumbent; competitive by later standards, but the tilt was already structural.

presidential.summary: Observers representing the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, cited what they called abuses of government resources, bias in the state media and instances of ballot stuffing on election day.
presidential.caveat: Serious opposition candidates declined or were kept off the air; observers found the campaign 'did not adequately reflect' democratic principles.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Russia on 2 March 2008. Incumbent president Vladimir Putin was ineligible to run for a third term.
presidential.caveat: A managed handover: Putin's chosen successor faced no genuine opposition and no real campaign.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Russia on 4 March 2012. There were five officially registered candidates: four representatives of registered parties, and one nominal independent.
presidential.caveat: Held amid mass protests over the rigged 2011 Duma vote, with credible fraud findings and the strongest opponents excluded.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Russia on 18 March 2018. Incumbent president Vladimir Putin was eligible to run.
presidential.caveat: The leading opposition figure, Alexei Navalny, was barred from the ballot; observers reported widespread irregularities.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Russia from 15 to 17 March 2024. It was the eighth presidential election in the country.
presidential.caveat: A wartime ritual, not an election: every genuine opponent was dead, imprisoned, exiled or barred, voting was extended into occupied Ukrainian territory, and the announced result was the highest in post-Soviet history.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in the Russian Empire from 26 March to 20 April 1906. At stake were the 477 seats in the State Duma of the Russian Empire, the legislative assembly.
legislative.caveat: Elected indirectly through class-weighted curiae under an autocracy — yet genuinely contested; the defiant Kadet-led First Duma was dissolved within 73 days.

legislative.label: January 1907
legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in the Russian Empire between 21 January and 1 March 1907. The Trudoviks emerged as the largest bloc in the second State Duma, winning 104 of the 518 seats.
legislative.caveat: Elected under the same class-weighted curial system; the radical Second Duma lasted barely three months before Stolypin dissolved it and rewrote the electoral law.

legislative.label: October 1907
legislative.summary: In June 1907, the Duma was forcibly dissolved by the Russian government, and some of its deputies arrested. Following the dissolution, the laws regarding elections were amended to favour wealthy pro-government Russians.
legislative.caveat: Held under the June 1907 electoral law, drastically re-weighted toward landowners and the wealthy — a franchise engineered to produce a loyal chamber.

legislative.summary: Around 51% of those elected were nobles, the highest during the Tsarist era. Both the right- and left-wing increased their representation in the Duma; right-wing candidates won 153 seats and left-wingers 152, whilst the centrists, including the Union of October 17, were reduced to 130 seats.
legislative.caveat: Held under Stolypin's restricted franchise, with heavy administrative interference in the voting.

legislative.summary: Elections to the Russian Constituent Assembly were held on 25 November 1917. Organized as a result of events in the February Revolution, the elections took place two months after they had been originally meant to occur.
legislative.caveat: A free, universal-suffrage election — Russia's first, and its last until 1991. The assembly it produced was dissolved by the Bolsheviks after a single day's sitting.

legislative.summary: Elections to the 9th All-Russian Congress of Soviets were held in the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic in the spring of 1921 (not to be confused with the 10th Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks)).
legislative.caveat: Indirect elections to the Congress of Soviets under consolidating Bolshevik power: non-party candidates could still stand, opposition parties could not.

legislative.summary: The Congress of Soviets was convened following the end of the main hostilities of the Russian Civil War, when the overwhelming number of White Army forces were defeated.
legislative.caveat: An indirect, single-party vote of the early Soviet state, on a class-weighted franchise that disenfranchised whole categories of citizens. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in the Soviet Union in 1924 to elect members of the Congress of Soviets. Some of the citizenry were not enthusiastic about elections in rural areas held the same year, for a number of varied reasons, possibly including reduced faith in the Soviets, which would increase in later years.
legislative.caveat: An indirect, single-party vote of the early Soviet state, on a class-weighted franchise that disenfranchised whole categories of citizens. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: A General Election was going on in Russia during my stay this year. Save for the reports in the news-papers, one would hardly have suspected it ...
legislative.caveat: An indirect, single-party vote of the early Soviet state, on a class-weighted franchise that disenfranchised whole categories of citizens. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: The elections were noteworthy for their rowdiness and elements of political opposition. Within the Communist Party, the Left Opposition attempted to run rival candidates against the officially nominated Communist candidates, while outside the party the Russian Orthodox Church attempted to create an organized opposition with religious candidates.
legislative.caveat: An indirect, single-party vote of the early Soviet state, on a class-weighted franchise that disenfranchised whole categories of citizens. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Supreme Soviet elections were held in the Soviet Union on 12 December 1937. It was the first election held under the 1936 Soviet Constitution, which had formed the Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union to replace the old legislature, the Congress of Soviets of the Soviet Union.
legislative.caveat: A single-candidate ritual of the Soviet state: one party-approved name per seat, with announced turnout near 100%. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Supreme Soviet elections were held in the Soviet Union on 10 February 1946. Originally scheduled for December 1941, the elections were delayed due to the outbreak of war with Germany in June of that year.
legislative.caveat: A single-candidate ritual of the Soviet state: one party-approved name per seat, with announced turnout near 100%. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: They were the last in the Soviet Union to be held before Mikhail Gorbachev's policies of perestroika and demokratizatsiya resulted in partially free elections in 1989. They were also the last direct elections to the Supreme Soviet, as in 1989 deputies were elected to the Congress of People's Deputies, who then elected the Supreme Soviet.
legislative.caveat: A single-candidate ritual of the Soviet state: one party-approved name per seat, with announced turnout near 100%. Recorded here as history, not as an election.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in the Soviet Union on 26 March 1989 to elect members of the Congress of People's Deputies, with run-offs on 2, 9 and 20 April and 14 and 23 May. They were the first partially free nationwide elections held in the Soviet Union, and would be the last national elections held in that country before its dissolution in 1991.
legislative.caveat: Semi-free by design: a third of the seats were reserved for the CPSU and its organisations, but the contested districts offered the first genuine choice on a Soviet ballot since 1917.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Russia on 12 December 1993 to elect all 450 seats of the 1st State Duma of the Russian Federation. Additionally, the elections were the first and only instance of direct elections to the Federation Council, with future members appointed by provincial legislatures and governors.
legislative.caveat: Held weeks after tanks shelled the old parliament, with several opposition parties and newspapers banned — yet genuinely competitive among those allowed to run, and won on the party lists by Zhirinovsky's LDPR.

legislative.summary: The anti-government Communist Party won a total of 157 seats, the most deputies of any single bloc in the chamber. The pro-government Our Home – Russia came second with 55 seats, with the far-right Liberal Democratic Party of Russia falling to third place with 51.

legislative.knownAs: The election that made Putin possible
legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Russia on 19 December 1999 to elect the 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower house of the Federal Assembly. Like in the previous elections in 1995, the electoral system resulted in many parties competing for the proportional seats and a significant number of independent deputies elected.

As expected, the pro-Vladimir Putin United Russia party received the most votes (38%) and won the most seats, gaining a plurality in the Duma. The Communist Party remained the second largest, though much reduced in strength.
legislative.caveat: Competitive but tilted: observers judged the campaign 'free but not fair', with state television campaigning openly for United Russia.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Russia on 2 December 2007. At stake were the 450 seats in the 5th State Duma, the lower house of the Federal Assembly (the legislature).
legislative.caveat: A managed vote: Putin headed the United Russia list, opposition access was throttled, and the 7% threshold cleared the chamber of genuine opponents.

legislative.knownAs: The fraud that sparked the protests
legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Russia on 4 December 2011. At stake were the 450 seats in the 6th State Duma, the lower house of the Federal Assembly (the legislature).
legislative.caveat: Marred by documented ballot-box fraud — the trigger for the largest protests of the Putin era.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Russia on 18 September 2016, having been brought forward from 4 December. At stake were the 450 seats in the State Duma of the 7th convocation, the lower house of the Federal Assembly.
legislative.caveat: A managed vote on a demobilised electorate: turnout fell below 48%, and United Russia took three-quarters of the seats with under half the vote.

legislative.summary: Legislative elections were held in Russia from 17 to 19 September 2021. At stake were 450 seats in the 8th convocation of the State Duma, the lower house of the Federal Assembly.
legislative.caveat: Held with Navalny's movement outlawed as 'extremist', independent candidates barred from the ballot and tactical-voting tools suppressed — a managed vote, not a free one.
